<pb n="36"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta> would be established, it would depend on the desire to prove it. If something comes from somewhere, goes somewhere, and moves upwards, then <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss> would be beginningless; however, that is not the case. If there were no permanent thing at all, what would be the impermanent? Both the permanent and the impermanent would be eliminated.

If the world had a limit, how could there be a future world? If the world had no limit, how could there be a future world? Since the continuum of the <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates of experience</gloss> is like the flame of a lamp, therefore, both having a limit and having no limit are unreasonable.

If the former <note>referring to the past life or aggregate</note> were to perish, and if, depending on this aggregate, that aggregate did not arise, then the world would have a limit. If the former did not perish, and if, depending on this aggregate, that aggregate did not arise, then the world would have no limit.

If one part had a limit and one part had no limit, then the world would be both limited and unlimited. That too is not reasonable. How could one part of the <term>upadatr</term> <gloss>the appropriator or grasper</gloss> perish while another part does not perish? That is unreasonable. How could one part of the <term>upadana</term> <gloss>the appropriated or the fuel</gloss> perish while another part does not perish? That also is unreasonable.

If both limited and unlimited were established, then "neither limited nor unlimited" would depend on the desire to prove it. Furthermore, because all things are empty, at what time, regarding what, and from what would views such as permanence and so forth arise?

This concludes the twenty-seventh chapter, called the Examination of Views.

I prostrate to Gautama, who, moved by compassion, taught the sacred Dharma in order to abandon all views.

<pb n="37"/> The Root Verses on the Middle Way, called "Wisdom" <note>original: "Mulamadhyamakakarika-prajña"</note>, which establishes the <term>Abhidharma</term> <gloss>Higher Knowledge</gloss> of the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss>, correctly demonstrates the reality of the ultimate truth, and clarifies the method of the <term>Prajñaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss>. 

It was composed by the great master, the noble Nagarjuna, who possesses irresistible wisdom and compassion, who clarifies the method of the unsurpassed vehicle of the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus Gone One</gloss>, and who, after achieving the stage of Perfect Joy <note>the first bhumi or level of a Bodhisattva</note>, departed for the Land of Bliss <note>Sukhavati</note>. In the world system called Clear Light, he will become the <term>Tathagata</term> called Source of Wisdom Light.

By the command of the great king, the supreme sovereign Lha Tsanpo, it was translated, edited, and finalized by the great Indian <term>Madhyamika</term> <gloss>Middle Way Scholar</gloss> master Jnanagarbha and the chief editor and translator, the monk Chokro Lui Gyaltsen. This work contains twenty-seven chapters and four hundred and forty-nine verses <note>original: "shloka"</note>. It is divided into one and a half volumes <note>original: "bampo"</note>.

Later, in the center of the Rinchen Bapa temple in the peerless city of Kashmir, the Kashmiri master Hasumati and the Tibetan translator Patsab Nyima Drak revised it during the time of the sovereign Phagpa Lha, in accordance with the commentary called the "Clear Words" <note>the Prasannapada by Chandrakirti</note>. Subsequently, in the Rasa Trulnang temple <note>the Jokhang in Lhasa</note>, the Indian master Kanaka and the same translator conducted the final great editorial review.
</translation>

<summary>This text concludes the twenty-seventh chapter of Nagarjuna's Root Verses on the Middle Way, refuting fixed views on the nature of the world and the self. The colophon details the work's authorship by Nagarjuna and its translation history involving masters like Jnanagarbha and Patsab Nyima Drak.</summary>

<keywords>Nagarjuna, Madhyamaka, Emptiness, Samsara, Colophon, Gautama Buddha, Jnanagarbha, Patsab Nyima Drak, Tibet, Kashmir</keywords>
